metadata.purpose: Canonical taxonomy for the economic-intelligence interpretation layer built on top of the completed industry corpus.

working_thesis: The US economy in 2025-2026 is being reorganized by overlapping pressures: labor scarcity, demographic aging, AI and compute buildout, consumer bifurcation, channel migration, politicized supply chains, compliance load, higher cost of capital, and consolidation.

domains.title: Industrial
domains.description: How the physical economy is being rebuilt through tariffs, capex, infrastructure, real-estate rotation, compliance burden, and margin pressure.
questions: Where is capex flowing and what physical bottlenecks shape it?
Which industries are being repriced by tariffs, power, labor, or real-estate math?
Where does scale or asset ownership matter more than craftsmanship or fragmentation?

forces.title: Atoms Strike Back
forces.signature: Trade war and tariffs force reshoring, nearshoring, and inventory hoarding — physical supply chains get expensive and political, and whoever moves fastest to nearshore wins.

subforces.title: The auto tariff shock
subforces.angle: 2025 tariffs and the EV transition force the whole auto supply chain to reorder toward Mexico.

subforces.title: The EV transition & legacy parts
subforces.angle: Electrification voids some parts and creates others; suppliers must pick a side.

subforces.title: Metals behind the tariff wall
subforces.angle: Steel and aluminum tariffs ripple into every downstream builder and maker.

subforces.title: The materials of everything
subforces.angle: Basic materials get repriced by tariffs, energy, and reshoring.

subforces.title: Reshoring advanced manufacturing
subforces.angle: Defense, reshoring mandates, and supply-chain security pull advanced manufacturing home.

subforces.title: Appliances & durable goods
subforces.angle: Durable-goods makers weigh tariff costs against nearshoring and automation.

subforces.title: Food's tariff exposure
subforces.angle: Food processing and ag ride commodity and trade-war volatility.

subforces.title: The retail import shock
subforces.angle: Import-heavy retail eats tariff costs or passes them to shoppers.

subforces.title: Atoms strike back
subforces.angle: Capstone: the physical supply chain got political; nearshoring and domestic makers win, thin-margin importers lose.

forces.title: The Great Consolidation
forces.signature: Capital rolls up fragmented Main Street — PE, franchises, REITs, and scale leaders absorb the independents, and financialization wins while owner-operators exit.

subforces.title: Private equity in medicine
subforces.angle: PE rolls up practices and clinics, chasing scale and billing power.

subforces.title: Scale in devices & generics
subforces.angle: Med-tech and generics consolidate to survive pricing pressure.

subforces.title: The franchise roll-up
subforces.angle: Franchising and PE turn local services into scaled, financialized platforms.

subforces.title: Consolidating boring services
subforces.angle: Professional and boring-but-essential services get rolled into regional platforms.

subforces.title: Scale wins in retail
subforces.angle: A few big-box leaders capture the category; independents fold.

subforces.title: Scale in food & drink
subforces.angle: Distribution and production consolidate; craft and independents get bought or squeezed.

subforces.title: REITs own the ground
subforces.angle: Institutional capital owns the real assets and rents them back.

subforces.title: IP & catalogs as assets
subforces.angle: Rights and catalogs get financialized into yield-bearing assets.

subforces.title: The great consolidation
subforces.angle: Capstone: capital rolls up the fragmented economy; scale and financialization win, independent owners exit.

forces.title: The Real-Estate Reckoning
forces.signature: Hybrid work broke the office and higher rates broke the math — capital rotates from offices to logistics, data centers, and housing, and a debt wall forces the reckoning.

subforces.title: The office crisis
subforces.angle: Hybrid work and vacancies gut office values; a maturity wall forces losses.

subforces.title: Adaptive reuse & conversion
subforces.angle: Dead offices and malls get converted — a remodeling and construction opportunity.

subforces.title: The housing squeeze
subforces.angle: High rates freeze buying and pressure multifamily even as housing stays scarce.

subforces.title: Logistics & data centers
subforces.angle: Capital flows to warehouses and data centers — the assets with demand.

subforces.title: Owning the land
subforces.angle: Land and ground-lease models become the quiet, durable real-estate bet.

subforces.title: Hotels as real estate
subforces.angle: Lodging bifurcates and gets financialized as an asset class.

subforces.title: Retail's property fallout
subforces.angle: Store closures dump retail real estate onto the market for reuse.

subforces.title: The commercial-debt wall
subforces.angle: A wave of maturing CRE loans refinancing at higher rates is the sector's tail risk.

subforces.title: Building costs bite
subforces.angle: Tariffs, labor, and rates raise the cost to build anything new.

subforces.title: The real-estate reckoning
subforces.angle: Capstone: work and rates broke the old real-estate math; logistics, data, and housing win, offices lose.

forces.title: The Compliance Tax
forces.signature: A patchwork of AI, privacy, climate, and cyber rules turns compliance into a rising cost — it favors scale, feeds the consultants, and prices out the small operator.

subforces.title: The bank compliance load
subforces.angle: Capital, KYC, and consumer rules make compliance a moat for big banks.

subforces.title: Insurance & the regulators
subforces.angle: State-by-state rules and new risks make insurance a compliance-heavy, data-heavy game.

subforces.title: Healthcare's paperwork machine
subforces.angle: Regulation and reimbursement rules make admin a huge, growing cost center.

subforces.title: Data, privacy & cyber
subforces.angle: Privacy and cyber rules raise the cost of holding data — and create a security market.

subforces.title: Who profits from the rules
subforces.angle: Lawyers, auditors, and accountants sell the compliance the rules require.

subforces.title: Environmental & climate rules
subforces.angle: Climate and environmental mandates create work and cost in equal measure.

subforces.title: The small-operator squeeze
subforces.angle: Compliance cost is fixed, so it hits small firms hardest and pushes consolidation.

subforces.title: Governing the algorithms
subforces.angle: New AI-governance rules land first on data, credit, and software.

subforces.title: The compliance tax
subforces.angle: Capstone: rules multiply into a tax that favors scale and feeds advisors; small operators pay the most.

forces.title: The Margin Vise
forces.signature: Labor, materials, energy, and tariffs rise faster than pricing power — margins compress, and only the automated, the premium, or the locked-in escape the squeeze.

subforces.title: The food-producer squeeze
subforces.angle: Commodity, labor, and energy costs outrun what packaged-food makers can charge.

subforces.title: The sweet-goods squeeze
subforces.angle: Cocoa, sugar, and dairy inflation crush indulgent-category margins.

groups.label: B · Serving food at a loss-leader price

subforces.title: The restaurant margin trap
subforces.angle: Wage and food inflation collide with price-sensitive diners.

subforces.title: The drinks squeeze
subforces.angle: Input costs and flat demand compress beverage margins.

groups.label: C · Where the lock-in defends the margin

subforces.title: The lock-in defense
subforces.angle: Captive locations and bundles defend margin where switching is hard.

subforces.title: Utility-like resilience
subforces.angle: Regulated, contracted, or essential businesses hold margin better.

subforces.title: Automating the cost away
subforces.angle: Automation is the main lever left to protect margin from labor inflation.

subforces.title: Premium as the shield
subforces.angle: Trading up to premium is the other way to keep pricing power.

subforces.title: The margin vise
subforces.angle: Capstone: costs rise faster than prices; automate, premiumize, or lock customers in — or watch margin vanish.

forces.title: The Pricing-Power Collapse
forces.signature: Medicare cuts and payer power strip pricing from providers and device makers — volume rises with aging, but the price per unit keeps falling, and only scale survives.

subforces.title: Death by reimbursement cut
subforces.angle: Year after year, Medicare trims the rate while costs rise — a structural margin squeeze.

subforces.title: The specialist squeeze
subforces.angle: Specialists face flat reimbursement and rising costs, pushing them into groups.

subforces.title: The device price grind
subforces.angle: Hospital consolidation and payers grind device prices down 1-2% a year.

subforces.title: Generic-drug deflation
subforces.angle: Relentless price erosion in generics rewards only the largest, lowest-cost makers.

groups.label: C · The payers hold the power

subforces.title: Who holds the purse
subforces.angle: Insurers and Medicare Advantage set prices and squeeze everyone downstream.

subforces.title: The independent-practice exodus
subforces.angle: Solo and small practices sell to systems and PE to survive the pricing squeeze.

subforces.title: Volume up, price down
subforces.angle: Aging drives volume, but falling per-unit prices and wage costs eat the gains.

subforces.title: The value-based bet
subforces.angle: Shifting to value-based, lower-cost sites of care is the industry's escape hatch.

subforces.title: The pricing-power collapse
subforces.angle: Capstone: reimbursement and payer power strip pricing from healthcare; volume grows but only scale survives.

operators.title: The Specialty Manufacturer
operators.thesis: Small industrial manufacturers can be defensible when they make narrow, specified products that customers cannot easily substitute.
operator_questions: Is demand driven by replacement, regulation, or specification rather than discretionary volume?
Can automation or procurement improve margin without new plant risk?
Are tariffs and input costs pass-throughable?

operators.title: The Distribution Middleman
operators.thesis: Distribution businesses are attractive when inventory, credit, technical knowledge, or local availability makes the middleman hard to remove.
operator_questions: Is the distributor providing credit, speed, expertise, or just taking a margin?
Can procurement scale improve gross margin?
Which customers can bypass the channel?

operators.title: The Regulated Admin Stack
operators.thesis: Complexity creates businesses: testing, claims, identity, forensic work, HR, and compliance software turn regulation into recurring demand.
operator_questions: Is the work mandatory, recurring, and hard to defer?
Can AI reduce fulfillment cost without increasing liability?
Are customers buying risk reduction or just a cheaper workflow?

domains.title: Consumer
domains.description: How households are reallocating spend across value, premium, health, convenience, channels, and experiences.
questions: Where are consumers trading down, and where do they still pay up?
Which categories are being reshaped by health, convenience, or status signaling?
Which parts of consumer demand are cyclical versus structurally re-ranked?

forces.title: The Health Reckoning
forces.signature: GLP-1 drugs, the sober-curious wave, and the retreat from sugar are rewriting what people eat and drink — volume shrinks, and only the health-aligned or premium survive.

groups.label: A · The drug that changed appetite

subforces.title: The GLP-1 shockwave
subforces.angle: Weight-loss drugs cut appetite and are already reshaping food, drink, and weight-loss demand.

subforces.title: Snacking under siege
subforces.angle: Indulgent, calorie-dense categories face structural demand pressure as appetites shrink and scrutiny rises.

subforces.title: The sober-curious wave
subforces.angle: Younger drinkers drink less; alcohol venues and makers face a structural, not cyclical, decline.

subforces.title: Spirits in contraction
subforces.angle: A boom-to-bust hangover: gluts, tariffs, and moderation hit premium spirits hard.

subforces.title: Functional & better-for-you drinks
subforces.angle: Sugar-free, functional, and 'better-for-you' positioning is the only growth lane left in beverages.

subforces.title: When diet meets convenience
subforces.angle: Health-conscious, convenient eating reshuffles who wins in packaged and prepared food.

subforces.title: What you drink now
subforces.angle: Coffee, milk alternatives, and snacks reposition around health and premium to hold volume.

subforces.title: Fast food's reckoning
subforces.angle: Value and indulgence collide with health scrutiny and GLP-1; chains reformulate or lose share.

subforces.title: Regulation & the warning label
subforces.angle: Health warnings, sugar rules, and scrutiny become a cost and a repositioning trigger.

subforces.title: The health reckoning
subforces.angle: Capstone: wellness and weight-loss drugs shrink volume across food and drink; health-aligned and premium win, vice loses.

forces.title: The Hollow Middle
forces.signature: The middle market collapses — shoppers split into premium and value, and anyone stuck selling undifferentiated mid-tier goods gets squeezed from both sides.

subforces.title: The department store falls
subforces.angle: The mid-tier anchor of retail hollows out as shoppers go luxury or discount.

subforces.title: The value floor
subforces.angle: Trading down powers dollar, convenience, and value formats.

subforces.title: The premium ceiling
subforces.angle: Affluent shoppers keep spending on jewelry, beauty, and status goods.

subforces.title: Apparel splits
subforces.angle: Fast-fashion and luxury grow; mid-price apparel chains close.

subforces.title: Footwear & the niche
subforces.angle: Specialty and athletic footwear thrive; generic mid-tier shoe retail shrinks.

subforces.title: Dining bifurcates
subforces.angle: Casual-dining middle empties as diners split between cheap fast food and premium experiences.

subforces.title: Hotels pick a lane
subforces.angle: Budget and luxury/experiential lodging grow; the mid-scale motel struggles.

subforces.title: Paying for the experience
subforces.angle: Consumers trade goods for experiences and premium live events.

subforces.title: Value's revenge: the dupe
subforces.angle: Cheap 'dupes' and private label eat the mainstream middle of consumer goods.

subforces.title: The hollow middle
subforces.angle: Capstone: the middle market is hollowing out; luxury and value win, undifferentiated mid-tier loses.

forces.title: The Channel Shift
forces.signature: The store stopped being where you buy — e-commerce, marketplaces, and direct-to-consumer hollow out physical retail, and only omnichannel or the experiential niche survives.

groups.label: A · The categories that went online first

subforces.title: Electronics go online
subforces.angle: Commodity electronics were the first to move online; specialty stores nearly vanished.

subforces.title: Media & hobby retail
subforces.angle: Amazon and marketplaces gutted these categories; survivors go experiential and expert.

subforces.title: Apparel & the try-before-you-buy problem
subforces.angle: Clothing and shoes shift online despite fit friction; stores become showrooms.

subforces.title: The marketplace eats the middle
subforces.angle: The platform takes a cut of everything and sets the terms of survival for sellers.

subforces.title: Direct-to-consumer brands
subforces.angle: Brands sell straight to shoppers, cutting the retailer out entirely.

subforces.title: Omnichannel or die
subforces.angle: Big-box survivors fuse online and store — ship-from-store, buy-online-pickup — or lose.

subforces.title: The experiential survivor
subforces.angle: Expertise, immediacy, and experience are the moats physical retail has left.

subforces.title: Tariffs & the de-minimis end
subforces.angle: Shein/Temu and the end of the de-minimis loophole reshape the price war online.

subforces.title: The closure wave
subforces.angle: Thousands of stores close a year; the real-estate and jobs fallout compounds.

subforces.title: The channel shift
subforces.angle: Capstone: the point of sale moved online; platforms and omnichannel scale win, standalone mid-market stores lose.

forces.title: The Margin Vise
forces.signature: Labor, materials, energy, and tariffs rise faster than pricing power — margins compress, and only the automated, the premium, or the locked-in escape the squeeze.

subforces.title: The food-producer squeeze
subforces.angle: Commodity, labor, and energy costs outrun what packaged-food makers can charge.

subforces.title: The sweet-goods squeeze
subforces.angle: Cocoa, sugar, and dairy inflation crush indulgent-category margins.

groups.label: B · Serving food at a loss-leader price

subforces.title: The restaurant margin trap
subforces.angle: Wage and food inflation collide with price-sensitive diners.

subforces.title: The drinks squeeze
subforces.angle: Input costs and flat demand compress beverage margins.

subforces.angle: Captive locations and bundles defend margin where switching is hard.

subforces.title: Utility-like resilience
subforces.angle: Regulated, contracted, or essential businesses hold margin better.

subforces.title: Automating the cost away
subforces.angle: Automation is the main lever left to protect margin from labor inflation.

subforces.title: Premium as the shield
subforces.angle: Trading up to premium is the other way to keep pricing power.

subforces.title: The margin vise
subforces.angle: Capstone: costs rise faster than prices; automate, premiumize, or lock customers in — or watch margin vanish.

operators.title: The Experiential Venue
operators.thesis: Experience businesses survive the channel shift when the venue itself is the product and utilization can be managed tightly.
operator_questions: Can utilization be smoothed across weekdays and seasons?
Does the concept have local scarcity or is it easy to copy?
Are labor, insurance, and rent rising faster than ticket yield?

operators.title: The Food Production Niche
operators.thesis: Niche food producers live between health-driven demand shifts, input-cost volatility, and retailer/wholesaler bargaining power.
operator_questions: Is this product riding health, premium, convenience, or indulgence?
Can input swings be hedged or passed through?
Does distribution create the moat or the squeeze?

operators.title: The Local Services Rollup
operators.thesis: Fragmented local service categories become better businesses when scheduling, pricing, labor, and marketing are centralized.
operator_questions: Can dispatch, booking, marketing, and procurement be centralized without killing local demand?
Is labor scarce enough that recruiting and retention are the real moat?
Can price increases be passed through without churn?

domains.title: Cultural & Social
domains.description: How identity, work, attention, status, and norms are changing behavior across labor, media, food, retail, and services.
questions: How are work identity, expertise, and junior labor changing?
How is status moving between goods, experiences, and digital mediation?
Which social changes are becoming economic demand shifts rather than niche behaviors?

forces.title: The Fractional Worker
forces.signature: Permanent jobs unbundle into gigs, fractional roles, and expert networks — the firm rents talent by the hour, and the platform in the middle takes the cut.

subforces.title: The expert, on demand
subforces.angle: Companies rent senior judgment by the call or the project instead of hiring it full-time.

subforces.title: Fractional leadership
subforces.angle: Fractional CFOs, CMOs, and coaches replace full-time executives at smaller firms.

subforces.title: Advice as a rented service
subforces.angle: Whole functions — HR, marketing, compliance — get rented from consultants instead of staffed.

groups.label: B · The platforms in the middle

subforces.title: Who places the talent
subforces.angle: Recruiters and brokers monetize the matching as work fragments.

subforces.title: Selling the credential
subforces.angle: Short-course and certification providers sell the fast credentials the gig market rewards.

subforces.title: The benefits gap
subforces.angle: Fractional work shifts benefits and stability onto the worker; insurers reprice the risk.

subforces.title: The firm gets thinner
subforces.angle: Professional firms lean on contractors and offshoring, thinning the permanent core.

subforces.title: The fractional worker
subforces.angle: Capstone: the unit of work shrinks from the job to the task; platforms and specialists win, stability loses.

operators.title: The Health Services Operator
operators.thesis: Healthcare service operators win when they manage reimbursement, staffing, referral flow, and compliance better than local independents.
operator_questions: Is payer mix improving or deteriorating?
Can clinician and caregiver labor be recruited reliably?
Does compliance complexity favor scale?

domains.title: Societal & Institutional
domains.description: How demographics, regulation, public funding, care burden, institutional risk, and labor supply are reorganizing the economy.
questions: Where do demographics create inevitable demand but constrained returns?
Where does regulation create drag, defensibility, or both?
Which sectors are really driven by reimbursement, staffing, or policy rather than pure market demand?

forces.title: The Graying Market
forces.signature: The boomers hit their care years — demand floods into everything age-related, but reimbursement cuts and a caregiver shortage cap the upside.

subforces.title: Joint repair & surgery
subforces.angle: Aging joints and eyes drive implant and outpatient-surgery volume; robotics is now standard of care but Medicare cuts squeeze the price.

subforces.title: When the senses fade
subforces.angle: Hearing and vision decline create steady demand; OTC hearing aids and retail optical reshape who captures it.

subforces.title: The chronic-disease machine
subforces.angle: Kidney and heart disease scale with age into recurring, consolidated, reimbursement-dependent care.

subforces.title: Senior housing at scale
subforces.angle: Boomer demand meets a bed shortage and a wage spiral; PE rolls up the fragment.

subforces.title: Care comes home
subforces.angle: The money rewards keeping seniors out of facilities; home care booms but can't hire fast enough.

subforces.title: The specialists of old age
subforces.angle: Age-skewed outpatient specialties ride the demographic wave while fighting reimbursement pressure.

groups.label: C · The money side of aging

subforces.title: Insuring a longer life
subforces.angle: Living longer turns into an annuity and long-term-care market — the balance-sheet side of aging.

subforces.title: The drug that rewrote aging
subforces.angle: GLP-1 drugs are the biggest force in aging health — remaking weight loss, cardio-metabolic care, and pharma.

subforces.title: Grey leisure & the active old
subforces.angle: Wealthy, active retirees spend on experiences and the outdoors — a real growth pocket.

subforces.title: Who pays for all this
subforces.angle: Medicare Advantage and insurers hold the purse; benefit cuts and cost control cap every provider's pricing.

subforces.title: The caregiver shortage
subforces.angle: The binding constraint isn't demand — it's the aides and nurses to serve it, and wages spiral.

subforces.title: The graying market
subforces.angle: Capstone: aging is a guaranteed demand wave, but labor and reimbursement decide who actually profits.

forces.title: The Labor Squeeze
forces.signature: Workers got scarce — wages spiral, the trades can't fill the gap, and whoever can automate or pay up wins while everyone else eats the margin hit.

subforces.title: The skilled-trades gap
subforces.angle: An aging trades workforce and few new entrants push wages up faster than contractors can pass them on.

subforces.title: The people who build things
subforces.angle: Construction demand meets a structural worker shortage; robots and prefab are the reluctant answer.

subforces.title: Hands for the infrastructure boom
subforces.angle: Federal money and mandates create work, but the workers to do it are the bottleneck.

subforces.title: The care-worker crunch
subforces.angle: Nurses and aides are the scarce input in a demographically guaranteed-demand sector.

subforces.title: Clinical labor everywhere
subforces.angle: Clinician shortages ripple through every corner of outpatient care.

subforces.title: The driver shortage
subforces.angle: Trucking's chronic driver churn collides with freight cycles; automation looms but isn't here yet.

subforces.title: Aviation's people problem
subforces.angle: Pilots, ground crew, and caterers are scarce and unionized; labor sets the cost floor.

subforces.title: The hospitality wage spiral
subforces.angle: Low-wage service work reprices upward; operators automate the counter or eat the margin.

subforces.title: Automate or eat the margin
subforces.angle: Where labor can be mechanized, it is; where it can't, margins compress.

subforces.title: Passing the wages on
subforces.angle: Service businesses try to pass wage inflation to customers — until price resistance bites.

subforces.title: The labor squeeze
subforces.angle: Capstone: labor is the new scarce resource; automation, wages, and consolidation are the three ways out.

forces.title: The Compliance Tax
forces.signature: A patchwork of AI, privacy, climate, and cyber rules turns compliance into a rising cost — it favors scale, feeds the consultants, and prices out the small operator.

subforces.title: The bank compliance load
subforces.angle: Capital, KYC, and consumer rules make compliance a moat for big banks.

subforces.title: Insurance & the regulators
subforces.angle: State-by-state rules and new risks make insurance a compliance-heavy, data-heavy game.

subforces.title: Healthcare's paperwork machine
subforces.angle: Regulation and reimbursement rules make admin a huge, growing cost center.

subforces.title: Data, privacy & cyber
subforces.angle: Privacy and cyber rules raise the cost of holding data — and create a security market.

subforces.title: Who profits from the rules
subforces.angle: Lawyers, auditors, and accountants sell the compliance the rules require.

subforces.title: Environmental & climate rules
subforces.angle: Climate and environmental mandates create work and cost in equal measure.

subforces.title: The small-operator squeeze
subforces.angle: Compliance cost is fixed, so it hits small firms hardest and pushes consolidation.

subforces.title: Governing the algorithms
subforces.angle: New AI-governance rules land first on data, credit, and software.

subforces.title: The compliance tax
subforces.angle: Capstone: rules multiply into a tax that favors scale and feeds advisors; small operators pay the most.

forces.title: The Pricing-Power Collapse
forces.signature: Medicare cuts and payer power strip pricing from providers and device makers — volume rises with aging, but the price per unit keeps falling, and only scale survives.

subforces.title: Death by reimbursement cut
subforces.angle: Year after year, Medicare trims the rate while costs rise — a structural margin squeeze.

subforces.title: The specialist squeeze
subforces.angle: Specialists face flat reimbursement and rising costs, pushing them into groups.

subforces.title: The device price grind
subforces.angle: Hospital consolidation and payers grind device prices down 1-2% a year.

subforces.title: Generic-drug deflation
subforces.angle: Relentless price erosion in generics rewards only the largest, lowest-cost makers.

groups.label: C · The payers hold the power

subforces.title: Who holds the purse
subforces.angle: Insurers and Medicare Advantage set prices and squeeze everyone downstream.

subforces.title: The independent-practice exodus
subforces.angle: Solo and small practices sell to systems and PE to survive the pricing squeeze.

subforces.title: Volume up, price down
subforces.angle: Aging drives volume, but falling per-unit prices and wage costs eat the gains.

subforces.title: The value-based bet
subforces.angle: Shifting to value-based, lower-cost sites of care is the industry's escape hatch.

subforces.title: The pricing-power collapse
subforces.angle: Capstone: reimbursement and payer power strip pricing from healthcare; volume grows but only scale survives.

operators.title: Care & Family Infrastructure
operators.thesis: Aging households, working parents, and health complexity create durable demand for care businesses, but labor and regulation cap returns.
operator_questions: Is demand demographic, cyclical, or policy-driven?
Where is the staffing bottleneck?
Does regulation protect scaled operators or punish them?

operators.title: The Health Services Operator
operators.thesis: Healthcare service operators win when they manage reimbursement, staffing, referral flow, and compliance better than local independents.
operator_questions: Is payer mix improving or deteriorating?
Can clinician and caregiver labor be recruited reliably?
Does compliance complexity favor scale?

operators.title: The Regulated Admin Stack
operators.thesis: Complexity creates businesses: testing, claims, identity, forensic work, HR, and compliance software turn regulation into recurring demand.
operator_questions: Is the work mandatory, recurring, and hard to defer?
Can AI reduce fulfillment cost without increasing liability?
Are customers buying risk reduction or just a cheaper workflow?

domains.title: Technological
domains.description: How AI, software, payments infrastructure, power demand, and data-center buildout are reshaping cost structures and winners.
questions: Where does AI substitute labor versus increase demand for infrastructure?
Which businesses own the rails, the software layer, or the compliance workflows around digitization?
Where is compute demand spilling into power, construction, telecom, and cooling chains?

forces.title: The Compute Super-Cycle
forces.signature: AI's hunger for power is reshaping the grid and everything plugged into it — whoever has electricity, land, and cooling near the data centers wins a once-in-a-generation buildout.

subforces.title: The data-center land rush
subforces.angle: AI compute demand turns land, power, and cooling into the scarce inputs of the decade.

subforces.title: The pipes to the internet
subforces.angle: Connectivity and hosting ride the same demand surge underneath the AI boom.

subforces.title: The software that runs on top
subforces.angle: Enterprise and data software monetize the compute build-out.

subforces.title: The generation scramble
subforces.angle: Data centers need firm power now; gas, solar, wind, and hydro all get pulled in.

subforces.title: The grid bottleneck
subforces.angle: Transmission and gas delivery — not generation — become the real constraint.

groups.label: C · The physical trades of the buildout

subforces.title: The electrical trades cash in
subforces.angle: Electricians, cooling contractors, and turbine makers are the picks-and-shovels of compute.

subforces.title: Concrete, steel & the shell
subforces.angle: Data centers are also a construction-materials story — concrete, steel, and heavy build.

subforces.title: When power gets scarce
subforces.angle: Whoever can't get power — homes, factories, small ISPs — pays more or waits.

subforces.title: Heat, water & the environment
subforces.angle: Cooling water and waste heat turn into constraints and opportunities.

subforces.title: The compute super-cycle
subforces.angle: Capstone: AI made electricity and land scarce again; the power-and-buildout chain is the trade of the decade.

forces.title: Money Gets Unbundled
forces.signature: Banking leaves the banks — it's embedded in apps, cards, and platforms — and scale, data, and the rails win while regional players and middlemen get squeezed.

subforces.title: The scale game in banking
subforces.angle: Deposits, tech, and compliance costs push banking toward a few giants.

subforces.title: The rails that tax every swipe
subforces.angle: Payment rails and card issuers take a cut of the whole economy's spending.

subforces.title: The Wall Street machine
subforces.angle: Capital markets and custody scale and financialize behind the scenes.

subforces.title: Lending without a bank
subforces.angle: Non-bank and embedded lenders route credit around the traditional bank.

subforces.title: Who grades your credit
subforces.angle: Scoring and rating is its own toll-taking layer, now AI-driven.

subforces.title: Advice gets commoditized
subforces.angle: Passive funds and robo-advice compress fees; scale and trust win.

subforces.title: Moving and holding the money
subforces.angle: Brokerage, custody, and the float are quiet, scaled, rate-sensitive businesses.

subforces.title: The regional-bank squeeze
subforces.angle: Rate whiplash, a CRE loan wall, and tech costs pressure smaller banks toward mergers.

subforces.title: Living and dying by the rate
subforces.angle: Fed rate moves reprice the whole lending stack — the swing factor for margins.

subforces.title: Money gets unbundled
subforces.angle: Capstone: finance splinters out of banks into rails, apps, and platforms; scale and data win, middlemen lose.

operators.title: The Regulated Admin Stack

operator_questions: Is the work mandatory, recurring, and hard to defer?
Can AI reduce fulfillment cost without increasing liability?
Are customers buying risk reduction or just a cheaper workflow?

operators.title: The Distribution Middleman
operators.thesis: Distribution businesses are attractive when inventory, credit, technical knowledge, or local availability makes the middleman hard to remove.
operator_questions: Is the distributor providing credit, speed, expertise, or just taking a margin?
Can procurement scale improve gross margin?
Which customers can bypass the channel?

operators.title: The Specialty Manufacturer
operators.thesis: Small industrial manufacturers can be defensible when they make narrow, specified products that customers cannot easily substitute.
operator_questions: Is demand driven by replacement, regulation, or specification rather than discretionary volume?
Can automation or procurement improve margin without new plant risk?
Are tariffs and input costs pass-throughable?

domains.title: Operator & Business-Model Lenses
domains.description: How the force map translates into practical business archetypes and recurring operator questions.
questions: What actually drives margin durability in this business type?
Is the binding constraint labor, regulation, capital, demand, distribution, or procurement scale?
What kind of operator is advantaged by the current force environment?

forces.title: The Margin Vise
forces.signature: Labor, materials, energy, and tariffs rise faster than pricing power — margins compress, and only the automated, the premium, or the locked-in escape the squeeze.

subforces.title: The food-producer squeeze
subforces.angle: Commodity, labor, and energy costs outrun what packaged-food makers can charge.

subforces.title: The sweet-goods squeeze
subforces.angle: Cocoa, sugar, and dairy inflation crush indulgent-category margins.

groups.label: B · Serving food at a loss-leader price

subforces.title: The restaurant margin trap
subforces.angle: Wage and food inflation collide with price-sensitive diners.

subforces.title: The drinks squeeze
subforces.angle: Input costs and flat demand compress beverage margins.

groups.label: C · Where the lock-in defends the margin

subforces.title: The lock-in defense
subforces.angle: Captive locations and bundles defend margin where switching is hard.

subforces.title: Utility-like resilience
subforces.angle: Regulated, contracted, or essential businesses hold margin better.

subforces.title: Automating the cost away
subforces.angle: Automation is the main lever left to protect margin from labor inflation.

subforces.title: Premium as the shield
subforces.angle: Trading up to premium is the other way to keep pricing power.

subforces.title: The margin vise
subforces.angle: Capstone: costs rise faster than prices; automate, premiumize, or lock customers in — or watch margin vanish.

forces.title: The Great Consolidation
forces.signature: Capital rolls up fragmented Main Street — PE, franchises, REITs, and scale leaders absorb the independents, and financialization wins while owner-operators exit.

subforces.title: Private equity in medicine
subforces.angle: PE rolls up practices and clinics, chasing scale and billing power.

subforces.title: Scale in devices & generics
subforces.angle: Med-tech and generics consolidate to survive pricing pressure.

subforces.title: The franchise roll-up
subforces.angle: Franchising and PE turn local services into scaled, financialized platforms.

subforces.title: Consolidating boring services
subforces.angle: Professional and boring-but-essential services get rolled into regional platforms.

subforces.title: Scale wins in retail
subforces.angle: A few big-box leaders capture the category; independents fold.

subforces.title: Scale in food & drink
subforces.angle: Distribution and production consolidate; craft and independents get bought or squeezed.

subforces.title: REITs own the ground
subforces.angle: Institutional capital owns the real assets and rents them back.

subforces.title: IP & catalogs as assets
subforces.angle: Rights and catalogs get financialized into yield-bearing assets.

subforces.title: The great consolidation
subforces.angle: Capstone: capital rolls up the fragmented economy; scale and financialization win, independent owners exit.

forces.title: The Labor Squeeze
forces.signature: Workers got scarce — wages spiral, the trades can't fill the gap, and whoever can automate or pay up wins while everyone else eats the margin hit.

subforces.title: The skilled-trades gap
subforces.angle: An aging trades workforce and few new entrants push wages up faster than contractors can pass them on.

subforces.title: The people who build things
subforces.angle: Construction demand meets a structural worker shortage; robots and prefab are the reluctant answer.

subforces.title: Hands for the infrastructure boom
subforces.angle: Federal money and mandates create work, but the workers to do it are the bottleneck.

subforces.title: The care-worker crunch
subforces.angle: Nurses and aides are the scarce input in a demographically guaranteed-demand sector.

subforces.title: Clinical labor everywhere
subforces.angle: Clinician shortages ripple through every corner of outpatient care.

subforces.title: The driver shortage
subforces.angle: Trucking's chronic driver churn collides with freight cycles; automation looms but isn't here yet.

subforces.title: Aviation's people problem
subforces.angle: Pilots, ground crew, and caterers are scarce and unionized; labor sets the cost floor.

subforces.title: The hospitality wage spiral
subforces.angle: Low-wage service work reprices upward; operators automate the counter or eat the margin.

subforces.title: Automate or eat the margin
subforces.angle: Where labor can be mechanized, it is; where it can't, margins compress.

subforces.title: Passing the wages on
subforces.angle: Service businesses try to pass wage inflation to customers — until price resistance bites.

subforces.title: The labor squeeze
subforces.angle: Capstone: labor is the new scarce resource; automation, wages, and consolidation are the three ways out.

subforces.title: The pricing-power collapse

forces.title: The Channel Shift
forces.signature: The store stopped being where you buy — e-commerce, marketplaces, and direct-to-consumer hollow out physical retail, and only omnichannel or the experiential niche survives.

groups.label: A · The categories that went online first

subforces.title: Electronics go online
subforces.angle: Commodity electronics were the first to move online; specialty stores nearly vanished.

subforces.title: Media & hobby retail
subforces.angle: Amazon and marketplaces gutted these categories; survivors go experiential and expert.

subforces.title: Apparel & the try-before-you-buy problem
subforces.angle: Clothing and shoes shift online despite fit friction; stores become showrooms.

subforces.title: The marketplace eats the middle
subforces.angle: The platform takes a cut of everything and sets the terms of survival for sellers.

subforces.title: Direct-to-consumer brands
subforces.angle: Brands sell straight to shoppers, cutting the retailer out entirely.

subforces.title: Omnichannel or die
subforces.angle: Big-box survivors fuse online and store — ship-from-store, buy-online-pickup — or lose.

subforces.title: The experiential survivor
subforces.angle: Expertise, immediacy, and experience are the moats physical retail has left.

subforces.title: Tariffs & the de-minimis end
subforces.angle: Shein/Temu and the end of the de-minimis loophole reshape the price war online.

subforces.title: The closure wave
subforces.angle: Thousands of stores close a year; the real-estate and jobs fallout compounds.

subforces.title: The channel shift
subforces.angle: Capstone: the point of sale moved online; platforms and omnichannel scale win, standalone mid-market stores lose.

operators.thesis: Fragmented local service categories become better businesses when scheduling, pricing, labor, and marketing are centralized.
operator_questions: Can dispatch, booking, marketing, and procurement be centralized without killing local demand?
Is labor scarce enough that recruiting and retention are the real moat?
Can price increases be passed through without churn?

crosscuts.title: Labor Scarcity
crosscuts.description: Skilled trades, care work, logistics, and service labor remain binding constraints across otherwise unrelated industries.

crosscuts.title: Consumer Bifurcation
crosscuts.description: The middle market is hollowing out while value and premium positions both keep winning for different reasons.

crosscuts.title: AI and Automation
crosscuts.description: AI is a labor story, an infrastructure story, and a software/compliance story at the same time.

crosscuts.title: Demographic Aging
crosscuts.description: Aging creates reliable demand growth, but staffing, reimbursement, and care-delivery friction cap who captures the upside.

crosscuts.title: Capital and Scale
crosscuts.description: Higher rates and heavier compliance reward scale players and financial owners while squeezing independents and mid-sized operators.
